reviews.review:
I was really hyped for this game, wanting to see Ron Gilbert's take on the exciting genre of Action Roguelites.
I'm a fan of Vampire: Survivors, Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor, Risk of Rain 2, etc so if you also like those games, my opinion could perhaps be of use to you.

Unfortunately, it feels like the developer either declined to look at what other games in the genre do right, or intentionally decided to go a different way. In any case, the results are not at all as interesting as I had hoped.
You see, one thing that these games have in common is that different characters (or weapons), have a one "something" that makes playing with them radically differrent. Either it is a crazy AOE bonus, or an exciting projectile weapon, or an interesting melee mechanic, etc. 
So every time you start a new game or find a new unlocked weapon, it feels like the game is meant to be played in a totally different way, and it keeps it exciting and addictive to keep unlocking stuff. You cannot wait to farm some more coin or some more missions to unlock some other character, some other weapon, some other bonus.
Or, even more exciting, the crazy combination of some character bonus with some combo of weapon or bonuses that makes you a killing machine or something.

Death by Scrolling is the opposite to all of that.
All weapons found during the time I was playing this game were minor variations of the same concept, with upgrades to those weapons or unlocks limiting themselves to lame "+5% damage" or "+2% projectile speed".
The character moves very slowly. Enemies can be defeated, but there is little point to do so other than to get gold to finish the run. That is, the point of killing monster is not to get better and get crazy exciting bonuses or new weapons, which encourage you to risk and try to get the droppable gold they release, no. The point of killing monsters is to reach 5k gold and end the run. 
So, essentially, you are supposed to kill monsters to reach a Game Over screen. This is kinda the opposite of what you would want in one of these games.
It's not like finishing the run gives you crazy unlocks or permanent bonuses for subsequent runs, no. 
Maybe it unlocks some other character that is only different in graphic and in a lame "+5% movement" bonus or something like that.

Weapons and other bonuses or effects are extremely limited. They come with ammo (very little of it, like 18 shots or less), and after you have shot those, your character reverts back to some lame default weapon, or the effect just plainly disappears.
You got a cool crossbow that shoots 3 bolts per attack? Enjoy it will it lasts for a whole lot of 10 shots!
You found cool power up that lets you walk over water? Only for 10 steps, sorry.
It's as if the designer was terrified of giving cool stuff to the player and thought that the best gameplay was to go around with the default boring melee/ranged attack.

You pick up gems that are laying about, which is your usual source of permanent progression. It takes you tons of gems to unlock something.
It wouldn't be a problem if 
- The things to unlock were exciting. They aren't. They are supposed to be equippable buffs, but they are so tame and lame that there is nothing excited about it. "+5% damage" or "+1 extra heart" after having to gather about 50 gems for each of them, or more.
- The gameplay would be riveting, and you just got the gems along the way. If it was the case, you wouldn't mind that gathering gems was slow, and the permanent unlocks were tame, since it would just be a cherry on top of how much fun you are having. 

But it is not the case. The gameplay is extremely straightforward, unrewarding, and uninteresting.
You move up in an autoscrolling level that has a certain length. 
In the time it takes to reach the end, you kill enemies for gold (that they drop but you need to go and get it), find a few gems that you need to reach to pick up (which is not fun with a slow character in an autoscrolling game full with choke points and blocking scenery).

You kill enemies by picking cards that are laying around. The cards have a line of text on top of them describing what they do. But since the text is constantly moving, the screen is full of camera shake, projectiles, and enemies, and you need to be watching for the killing edge of the scrolling screen and for enemies and blocking scenery, there is no real time to read what the text says and decide whether you want or not those cards. So you either ignore them or pick them up almost at random. There is not time for choice for the player, so in that way, you remove choice from the player.

Then these cards have weapons or effects that last for a few auto-uses. Either ammo or steps, or hits. Etc. All in all, in less than a minute since you picked the card, it will be gone or replaced with something totally else.
At the end, you stop caring about what the cards are because they are mostly samey, mostly effimeral, and the entire point of killing enemies goes against your interest of the game itself (why would I want to "win" if I get mostly nothing out of winning?).

There is a quest system, if you can call it that. It is limited to an NPC telling you "Find my X", and then, during a run, you need to find that X item in the autoscrolling level and pick it up. The reward is usually just gold, which pushes you towards the Game Over screen. So, again, it is worth arguing whether you would actually want to do these quests.
Again, the point of the game should be to have fun as you play it, not to "win" the levels, which is just another form of Game Over.

I played the game for 1.5 hours, and in that time it convinced me that I had seen all that the game had to show. If that was not the case, then I apologize, but the game did a very poor job at hinting at the awesome mechanics and gameplay that I perhaps missed by not grinding it for 10 more hours.

You might be thinking why did I bother to write such a wall of text for a game that I hate.
The reason is that I don't hate the game. I was looking forward to it a lot.
And I have loved Ron Gilbert as a developer since he created Maniac Mansion and wrote his "Why Adventure Games Suck" essay.

But I think this game requires a time for introspection and that the developer writes a "Why Death by Scrolling Sucks" while other action roguelites don't suck at all. 
If he does, then he can reshape this game into something very fun and special. It wouldn't be the first game that has had a total comeback and new life after some reworking.

As it is, I cannot recommend it, even for its low price.
